1930: Uruguay hosted the first FIFA World Cup in 1930. Thirteen teams took part, and all 18 matches were played in Montevideo. The hosts, already twice Olympic champions, went on to win the inaugural title against their neighbours Argentina.

Only four European teams made the long Atlantic crossing. In Montevideo's southern winter, early games used smaller grounds while the Estadio Centenario was being completed. Its opening gave the new competition a vast stage and the home crowds a place to gather behind Uruguay.

France's Lucien Laurent scored the first goal in World Cup history against Mexico. Argentina's Guillermo Stábile then emerged as the tournament's leading scorer, while Uruguay won its group and built its campaign around captain José Nasazzi and midfielder José Leandro Andrade.

Argentina and Uruguay each won their semi-final 6–1, setting up a final between long-standing rivals from either side of the Río de la Plata. Argentina led 2–1 at half-time, but Uruguay's second-half attack overturned the match at the Centenario.

Goals from Pedro Cea, Victoriano Iriarte and Héctor Castro completed a 4–2 win. Uruguay became the first world champion, and a dramatic local rivalry gave the new tournament a memorable opening chapter.
1934: Italy hosted the second World Cup in 1934 and won the first title decided by a straight knockout tournament. Sixteen teams entered the final stage, with no group games or second chances. Defending champion Uruguay did not take part.

The tournament unfolded before large Italian crowds under Benito Mussolini's regime, which used the event for political display. Every match carried immediate elimination, lending even the opening round a different tension from the competition in Uruguay four years earlier.

Egypt became the first African team to play at a World Cup, while Brazil and the United States went out in their opening matches. Italy advanced past the United States and Spain, but needed a replay after its first quarter-final against the Spanish ended level.

The hosts edged Austria 1–0 in the semi-final. Czechoslovakia reached the Rome final after beating Germany 3–1, with Oldřich Nejedlý finishing the tournament as its top scorer. Antonín Puč put the Czechoslovaks ahead late in the title match.
Raimundo Orsi equalised for Italy before Angelo Schiavio scored in extra time. The 2–1 victory made Italy the first European world champion and completed a demanding run of close knockout matches.
1938: France hosted the 1938 World Cup, another straight knockout edition. Italy arrived as defending champion and became the first team to retain the trophy, beating Hungary in the Paris final. Brazil's adventurous attack supplied several of the tournament's most dramatic moments.

The French grounds saw open, high-scoring football. Brazil and Poland produced an extraordinary 6–5 match in Strasbourg, with the lead repeatedly under threat. The contest captured the unpredictable mood of an edition in which several teams scored freely.

Brazil's Leônidas led the scorers with seven goals as his team progressed through the draw. Italy took a steadier route, eliminating host France in the quarter-finals and relying on the finishing of Silvio Piola and Gino Colaussi.

Italy then beat Brazil 2–1 in the semi-final. Hungary reached the final from the other side of the bracket and replied quickly after Italy opened the scoring, but Colaussi and Piola each struck twice to keep the champions in command.
Italy won 4–2 and became the first side to win consecutive World Cups. War prevented another tournament until 1950, so the Paris final also closed the competition's first era.
1950: Brazil hosted the World Cup's return in 1950 after a twelve-year interruption caused by the Second World War. The title was decided by a final round-robin group, and Uruguay emerged as champion after beating Brazil in the last match at the Maracanã.

Huge crowds filled Brazil's grounds, especially the newly built Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro. The home team's prolific attack raised expectations with every round. By the last day, the stadium had become the setting for what many supporters expected to be a coronation.

The United States delivered an early shock by beating England 1–0. Brazil later overwhelmed Sweden 7–1 and Spain 6–1 in the final group, while Ademir de Menezes finished as the tournament's leading scorer. Uruguay had to battle through its own group matches to stay in contention.

Brazil needed only a draw in the final game and went ahead through Friaça. Uruguay, which had to win, equalised through Juan Alberto Schiaffino. With little time remaining, Alcides Ghiggia scored again and silenced the vast home crowd.

Uruguay's 2–1 victory brought a second world title. The reversal, remembered as the Maracanazo, remains one of the competition's most powerful examples of how quickly a seemingly certain outcome can change.
1954: Switzerland hosted the 1954 World Cup, a high-scoring edition that ended with West Germany's first title. Hungary entered the final unbeaten for years and had already beaten the Germans 8–3 in the group stage, making the result in Bern an immense upset.

Goals came in extraordinary numbers across the Swiss grounds. Austria's 7–5 quarter-final win over the hosts remains the highest-scoring match in World Cup history. Even strong leads could feel fragile, creating a restless atmosphere around the tournament's attacking sides.

Hungary began by scoring nine against South Korea and eight against West Germany. Sándor Kocsis finished with eleven goals, while Ferenc Puskás and his teammates survived demanding 4–2 knockout wins over Brazil and Uruguay to reach the final.

West Germany recovered from its heavy group defeat to make the same match. In rain-soaked Bern, Hungary went 2–0 ahead inside eight minutes. Max Morlock and Helmut Rahn quickly drew the Germans level before Rahn struck again late in the second half.
The 3–2 comeback became the Miracle of Bern. West Germany lifted its first World Cup, while Hungary's only defeat in the competition came in the match that decided the title.
1958: Sweden hosted the 1958 World Cup, where Brazil won its first title and 17-year-old Pelé emerged on the global stage. France's Just Fontaine set a record with thirteen goals, while the home side made its own memorable run to the final.

Swedish support grew as the hosts advanced, culminating in a semi-final victory over West Germany. Brazil offered a different attraction: Garrincha's dribbling, Didi's passing and Vavá's finishing surrounded the teenage Pelé with an array of attacking options.

Fontaine scored throughout France's campaign, including four goals in the third-place match. Pelé began making his mark in the knockout rounds, scoring the winner against Wales and then a hat-trick against France in the semi-final.

Sweden took an early lead in the Stockholm final, but Vavá struck twice to turn the game around. Pelé added two goals of his own, one after a deft flick over a defender and a volley, as Brazil pulled clear of the hosts.
Brazil won 5–2 for its first world title. The final crowned a fluent attacking team and began Pelé's extraordinary World Cup story.
1962: Chile hosted the 1962 World Cup after the devastating earthquake of 1960. Brazil arrived as champion and retained the title despite losing Pelé to injury early in the competition. The hosts also reached the semi-finals and finished third.

Chile's rebuilding gave the tournament a strong local meaning, while some matches were fiercely physical. The host team's 2–0 win over Italy became known as the Battle of Santiago. Its progress gave home crowds a reason to stay deeply involved after that notorious group game.

Pelé's injury against Czechoslovakia forced Brazil to adjust. Amarildo stepped in, and Garrincha became the decisive attacking figure. Chile defeated the Soviet Union in the quarter-finals, while Brazil moved past England with Garrincha scoring twice.

Garrincha struck twice more against Chile in the semi-final. Czechoslovakia, led by Josef Masopust, came through the other half of the draw and Masopust put his side ahead in the Santiago final. Brazil answered almost immediately through Amarildo.
Zito and Vavá completed a 3–1 Brazilian victory. Brazil became only the second team to retain the World Cup, while Chile beat Yugoslavia to secure third place before its home supporters.
1966: England hosted the 1966 World Cup and won its first title, defeating West Germany after extra time at Wembley. Sixteen teams competed, with Portugal and North Korea among the sides that gave the edition some of its most surprising results.

The tournament began amid an unlikely off-field drama: a dog named Pickles found the stolen Jules Rimet Trophy before a ball was kicked. As England advanced, Wembley became the centre of home expectation, and the packed final gave the hosts their largest stage.

North Korea eliminated Italy in the group stage and then raced into a 3–0 quarter-final lead against Portugal. Eusébio scored four times as Portugal recovered to win 5–3. His nine goals made him the tournament's leading scorer.

England reached the semi-final with a strong defence, then beat Portugal 2–1 through two Bobby Charlton goals. West Germany awaited at Wembley. Geoff Hurst and Martin Peters scored for England, but Wolfgang Weber's late equaliser made it 2–2 and forced extra time.

Hurst's next shot hit the bar and bounced near the line; the referee awarded the disputed goal. Hurst completed his hat-trick as England won 4–2. The decision and the home side's first world title remain inseparable from the story of the final.
1970: Mexico hosted the 1970 World Cup, the first widely broadcast in colour. Brazil won all six matches and claimed its third title, led by Pelé and an attacking cast that included Jairzinho, Gérson, Tostão and Rivellino.

Heat and altitude tested the players, while colour television carried the Mexican stadiums to new audiences. Brazil's group meeting with England produced Gordon Banks's remarkable save from Pelé's downward header, one of the tournament's most enduring images.

Brazil beat England 1–0 and continued through the knockout rounds. Jairzinho scored in every Brazilian match, a feat unique to this title run. Elsewhere, Gerd Müller led the tournament with ten goals as West Germany eliminated England in the quarter-finals.

Italy then beat West Germany 4–3 after extra time in a semi-final with five goals beyond the regulation ninety minutes. In the Mexico City final, Pelé headed Brazil ahead. Italy equalised, but the Brazilian attack regained control after the break.

Goals from Gérson, Jairzinho and Carlos Alberto made it 4–1. Brazil kept the Jules Rimet Trophy after its third title, and Carlos Alberto's finish to a sweeping team move became a lasting image of the champions.
1974: West Germany hosted and won the 1974 World Cup, the first played for the new FIFA World Cup Trophy. The Netherlands captivated audiences with Total Football, but Franz Beckenbauer's hosts recovered from an early setback to beat Johan Cruyff's side in the final.

The home campaign carried extra tension after East Germany beat West Germany in a politically charged group match. Dutch players kept changing positions and pressing opponents, creating a vivid contrast with the hosts' more controlled approach as the teams moved toward a possible meeting.

West Germany won all three matches in the second group phase. The Netherlands beat Argentina 4–0 and Brazil 2–0, while Poland also impressed: Grzegorz Lato scored seven goals and his side eventually finished third.

The Dutch reached the Munich final after those commanding second-round wins. They won a penalty before a West German player had touched the ball, and Johan Neeskens converted. Paul Breitner answered from the spot before Gerd Müller turned the match in the hosts' favour.
West Germany held on for a 2–1 win and its second world title. Cruyff's Netherlands left without the trophy, but its fluid style became one of the tournament's most influential legacies.
1978: Argentina hosted and won the 1978 World Cup, claiming its first title against the Netherlands. Mario Kempes became the tournament's leading scorer, while the event unfolded under the country's military dictatorship.

Blue-and-white paper filled Argentine stadiums and home crowds followed the team closely. The military government also sought to use the competition for its own image, a political setting that remains part of the edition's history even in accounts of the celebrations.

Argentina advanced from the first group stage alongside Italy. Kempes did not score in that opening phase, but began finding the net in the second. Elsewhere, Scotland's Archie Gemmill scored a memorable solo goal in a 3–2 win over the Netherlands, though his side still went out.

Kempes scored twice as Argentina beat Poland, then twice more in the 6–0 win over Peru that sent the hosts to the final. The Netherlands reached a second consecutive title match and drew level in Buenos Aires through Dick Nanninga after Kempes had opened the scoring.

Rob Rensenbrink hit the post late in normal time, but Kempes struck again in extra time before Daniel Bertoni sealed a 3–1 win. Argentina celebrated its first world title in an atmosphere inseparable from the country's political crisis.
1982: Spain hosted the first 24-team World Cup in 1982. Italy recovered from three opening draws to win a third title, with Paolo Rossi's late burst of goals transforming its campaign. The expanded format also brought memorable upsets and a dispute over the final first-round group games.

The Spanish edition swung between attacking spectacle and frustration. Hungary beat El Salvador 10–1, while Algeria defeated West Germany and Chile yet was eliminated after West Germany's narrow win over Austria. The controversy led to simultaneous final group kickoffs in later editions.

Italy advanced despite its three draws and found form in the second group phase. Rossi scored a hat-trick in a 3–2 win over a Brazil side led by Sócrates, Zico and Falcão, abruptly ending one of the tournament's most admired attacking runs.

Rossi then scored twice against Poland in the semi-final. West Germany survived a 3–3 semi-final against France on penalties, setting up the Madrid final. Rossi arrived there with five goals from Italy's previous two matches and the scoring lead within reach.

Rossi broke the deadlock, and Marco Tardelli and Alessandro Altobelli extended Italy's lead before West Germany replied. The 3–1 victory gave Italy its third title; Rossi finished with six goals and Tardelli's exuberant celebration became a defining image.
1986: Mexico hosted the 1986 World Cup after Colombia withdrew. Argentina won its second title under Diego Maradona's leadership, while England's Gary Lineker finished as the tournament's leading scorer with six goals.

Huge crowds, especially at the Azteca, gave the competition noise and colour. The altitude and midday heat shaped the experience for players, while a series of dramatic knockout games kept attention on more than the eventual champions.

Denmark's exciting group-stage run ended in a 5–1 defeat by Spain. France beat Brazil on penalties in a tense quarter-final, and Lineker's goals carried England into a meeting with Argentina. Maradona had already established himself as the centre of his side's play.

Against England, Maradona scored first with a handball missed by the officials, then after a breathtaking run from his own half. He scored both goals against Belgium in the semi-final to take Argentina into the final against West Germany.

The Germans recovered from 2–0 down, but Maradona released Jorge Burruchaga for the winning goal in a 3–2 final. Argentina claimed its second world title, and Maradona's two contrasting goals against England became the edition's lasting images.
1990: Italy hosted the 1990 World Cup, which West Germany won by beating Argentina in a rematch of the previous final. Cameroon supplied the breakthrough story, reaching the quarter-finals, while Italy's Salvatore Schillaci became an unexpected scoring star.

Italian stadiums provided an impressive setting, though many matches were tight and low scoring. Roger Milla's corner-flag celebrations gave Cameroon's run a joyful character that stood out against the caution of several knockout contests.

Cameroon stunned defending champion Argentina in the opener and later eliminated Colombia before England stopped it in a dramatic quarter-final. Schillaci's goals carried the hosts through the draw; he ultimately scored six and received the Golden Ball.

Argentina beat Yugoslavia and then Italy on penalties to reach the final. West Germany also needed a shootout against England in its semi-final. The Rome decider remained tense, and Argentina finished with nine players after two dismissals.
Andreas Brehme converted a late penalty for a 1–0 West German win and a third world title. Cameroon's breakthrough and the narrow final left sharply different memories of the same tournament.
1994: The United States hosted the 1994 World Cup, attracting enormous crowds as Brazil won its fourth title. Bulgaria and Sweden reached the semi-finals, while the final against Italy became the first to be decided by a penalty shootout.

Large American stadiums and summer heat gave the edition a distinctive setting. Supporters watched unexpected challengers progress alongside the traditional powers, and Brazil's Romário gave a disciplined team moments of attacking flair.

Oleg Salenko scored five in one match against Cameroon, a World Cup record. He and Bulgaria's Hristo Stoichkov finished level on six goals, even though Russia went out after the groups. Bulgaria then eliminated defending champion Germany on its way to the last four.

Brazil edged the Netherlands 3–2 in the quarter-finals, with Bebeto celebrating his goal by rocking his arms like a cradle. Roberto Baggio's decisive strikes carried Italy through the other half of the draw, setting up a final between two three-time champions in Pasadena.

Neither team scored in 120 minutes. Brazil won the shootout after Baggio's last kick flew over the bar, becoming the first four-time world champion and giving the tournament one of its most recognisable closing images.
1998: France hosted the first 32-team World Cup in 1998 and won its first title. Croatia finished third in its debut as an independent nation, while Brazil returned to the final before losing 3–0 to the hosts in Paris.

The expanded field brought new combinations of teams and stories. Croatia's run became a source of national pride, and Michael Owen's solo goal against Argentina offered England a brilliant moment before its shootout exit.

Croatia beat Germany 3–0 in the quarter-finals, with Davor Šuker eventually finishing as the tournament's top scorer on six goals. Brazil advanced through the other side of the draw, and Ronaldo's performances earned him the Golden Ball.

France needed Laurent Blanc's golden goal to beat Paraguay and penalties to get past Italy. Lilian Thuram then scored his only two international goals in the semi-final against Croatia, overturning Šuker's opener and sending the hosts to meet Brazil.

Zinédine Zidane headed in twice in the final before Emmanuel Petit completed a 3–0 victory. France's first world title brought a national celebration, with Zidane's goals the clearest images of its triumph.
2002: South Korea and Japan co-hosted the 2002 World Cup, the first staged in Asia. Brazil won all seven matches to claim a fifth title, while Senegal and South Korea delivered two of the competition's most surprising runs.

Red-clad crowds followed South Korea from city to city, giving the co-hosts' campaign a striking visual presence. New stadiums and unfamiliar settings broadened the tournament's reach, and Senegal's debut added another source of excitement after the opening match.

Senegal stunned defending champion France 1–0 and went on to the quarter-finals. South Korea eliminated Italy with a golden goal, then beat Spain on penalties to reach the semi-finals, where Germany finally stopped its run.

Brazil's attack combined Ronaldo's finishing with Rivaldo's movement and Ronaldinho's creativity. Ronaldo scored in the semi-final against Türkiye to set up a final with Germany, whose goalkeeper Oliver Kahn had been central to its own progress.

Ronaldo struck twice in Yokohama for a 2–0 win and finished with eight goals. Brazil took a record fifth crown, and his return to the final four years after the troubled 1998 decider supplied a fitting close.
2006: Germany hosted the 2006 World Cup, which Italy won for the fourth time. France reached the final through a strong knockout run led by Zinédine Zidane, while the hosts' own progress helped sustain a lively public festival.

Supporters filled fan zones and city squares across Germany. The host team's matches kept those public viewing areas busy into July, and the welcoming mood extended beyond the stadiums even as the competition tightened in its later rounds.

Miroslav Klose scored five times for Germany to lead the tournament. France came through Spain, Brazil and Portugal, with Zidane directing its play. Italy advanced with a defence that conceded only twice in seven matches.

Italy's semi-final against Germany remained scoreless until two late extra-time goals settled it. In the Berlin final, Zidane's chipped penalty put France ahead, but Marco Materazzi equalised. Deep in extra time Zidane was sent off for headbutting Materazzi.
Italy won the shootout 5–3 and claimed its fourth world title. The victory completed a disciplined team campaign, while Zidane's dismissal gave his last professional match a shocking final scene.
2010: South Africa hosted the first World Cup on African soil in 2010. Spain recovered from an opening defeat to win its first title, beating the Netherlands after extra time. Ghana's near miss in the quarter-finals supplied another defining story.

Vuvuzelas sounded through packed stadiums and made the tournament instantly recognisable. South African crowds welcomed teams from around the world, while Ghana's progress carried special hopes for an African semi-finalist.

Germany scored four against both England and Argentina, and Ghana reached the last eight against Uruguay. Luis Suárez handled a goal-bound shot near the end of extra time; Asamoah Gyan missed the resulting penalty and Uruguay won the shootout.

Spain steadied itself after losing to Switzerland, then beat Portugal, Paraguay and Germany by 1–0 scores. The Netherlands arrived at the Johannesburg final unbeaten and nearly went ahead when Arjen Robben broke through, but Iker Casillas saved.
Andrés Iniesta scored in the 116th minute for a 1–0 victory. Spain's patient run ended with its first world title and provided a dramatic close to the tournament's African debut.
2014: Brazil hosted the 2014 World Cup, but Germany won the title after delivering the hosts a devastating semi-final defeat. Argentina reached the final, while Colombia and Costa Rica produced memorable runs through the knockout stage.

Colourful home crowds gave the tournament energy, even as Brazil's expectations grew heavier. Colombia's James Rodríguez drew attention with his goals and celebrations, and Costa Rica's progress challenged pre-tournament assumptions about the field.

Costa Rica won a group containing Uruguay, Italy and England and went on to the quarter-finals. Rodríguez scored six times, including a spectacular turning volley against Uruguay. Brazil advanced too, but Neymar's injury in the quarter-final left the hosts without their leading attacker.

Germany then beat Brazil 7–1 in a semi-final that stunned the country; Miroslav Klose became the World Cup's all-time leading scorer during the match. Argentina beat the Netherlands on penalties to set up a final between the South American side and Germany.

In Rio de Janeiro, Mario Götze controlled André Schürrle's cross and scored in extra time for a 1–0 German win. Germany became the first European side to win a World Cup in the Americas, although the 7–1 semi-final remained the edition's most startling result.
2018: Russia hosted the 2018 World Cup, the first to use video assistant refereeing. France won its second title, beating Croatia in the final, while defending champion Germany exited in the group stage.

Packed Russian stadiums witnessed repeated swings in momentum. Belgium's comeback against Japan and England's renewed run to the semi-finals kept the knockout rounds lively, alongside the long series of close matches survived by Croatia.

Germany's early elimination opened the field. France beat Argentina 4–3 in the round of 16, with teenage Kylian Mbappé scoring twice. Belgium recovered from 2–0 down to beat Japan 3–2, then eliminated Brazil in the quarter-finals.

Croatia advanced past Denmark and Russia on penalties, then beat England in extra time to reach its first final. Luka Modrić directed the midfield throughout that demanding run, while France overcame Belgium in the other semi-final.

An own goal, an Antoine Griezmann penalty and strikes from Paul Pogba and Mbappé gave France a 4–2 win in Moscow. Its second title crowned a new generation, and Modrić's Croatia left with a historic runner-up finish.
2022: Qatar hosted the first World Cup in the Middle East in 2022, moving the competition to November and December. Argentina won its third title after a dramatic final against France, while Morocco became the first African and Arab semi-finalist.

Crowds from across the region filled the compact group of host cities. The winter schedule gave the edition a different rhythm, and Morocco's victories brought broad celebration among Arab and African supporters.

Saudi Arabia upset Argentina in the group stage, but Lionel Messi's side recovered. Japan beat Germany and Spain, and Morocco eliminated Spain on penalties before defeating Portugal to reach the semi-finals.

Argentina survived a tense quarter-final against the Netherlands on penalties and beat Croatia in the semi-final. France overcame Morocco to reach the title match. Messi scored twice there, while Kylian Mbappé's hat-trick repeatedly pulled France back into contention.
The final finished 3–3 after extra time before Argentina won the shootout 4–2. Messi completed his pursuit of a World Cup title, and Mbappé's eight goals earned the Golden Boot.
2026: Canada, Mexico and the United States hosted the first 48-team World Cup in 2026. The expanded competition added a round of 32, and Spain won its second title by beating defending champion Argentina after extra time.

The three-country setting gave supporters a tournament spread across a vast map. New arrivals and traditional powers shared the larger field, while long journeys and a new knockout round made the route to the final feel different from earlier editions.

Spain began with a draw against Cabo Verde but progressed from its group. In the knockout rounds it beat Austria and Portugal, while Kylian Mbappé's goals kept France prominent in the other part of the competition.

Spain then eliminated Belgium and France to reach the final. Argentina edged England in the semi-final, setting up a meeting of the previous champion and a Spanish side that had grown more secure as the rounds passed.
The final stayed level until Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute. Spain held on for a 1–0 win and its second world title, sixteen years after its first.
2030: The 2030 World Cup is planned as a centenary edition, one hundred years after the first tournament in Uruguay. Morocco, Portugal and Spain are the principal hosts, with one celebratory match each in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.

The opening plan gives supporters in South America a direct connection to 1930. Montevideo, where every match of the first World Cup was played, will host a centenary celebration, before the event moves to stadiums across North Africa and Europe.

Three centenary matches are scheduled for Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay. Uruguay's game will return the competition to Montevideo, while Argentina's role recalls its appearance in the first final and Paraguay's reflects its place in South American football history.

After those centenary games, play is due to continue in Morocco, Portugal and Spain. FIFA plans extra travel and rest time for teams involved in the South American matches, allowing them to cross the Atlantic before their next fixtures.
No matches have been played and no champion can be named. The tournament's defining results will emerge in 2030; for now, the six-country plan offers a way to mark a century of World Cup football.
